URL: https://dronecleaningthailand.com/en/guides/drone-cleaning-cost-thailand/
Guide · Cost 

# How much does drone building cleaning cost in Thailand?

 Every quote we give is based on a site survey, so this page does not publish a price list. It explains what makes the price go up or down, how a drone quote compares with the alternatives, and what to send us to get a reliable figure quickly.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Short answer: drone cleaning is priced per square metre, and the rate depends on six things: the surface to clean, the height, the access for the ground unit, the level of dirt, the material (glass, cladding, stone, tiles, solar modules) and the permits required for the site. On large glass or roof surfaces the drone is usually cheaper than rope access or scaffolding because it works at 500 to 800 m² per hour with a crew of two or three on the ground. On small or very detailed façades, a water-fed pole or rope access is often the better deal, and we say so.

## The six factors that set the price

### 1. Surface area

 The larger the surface, the lower the rate per m². Set-up (van, water production, perimeter, flight checks) takes the same time for 300 m² and for 3,000 m². Above a few thousand m², a multi-day job with the same set-up brings the rate down further.

### 2. Height and geometry

 A tethered drone does not care much about height up to the length of its tether; a 25 m façade and a 60 m façade cost about the same per m². Geometry matters more: a flat curtain wall is faster than a façade with deep balconies, louvres or canopies that the jet has to work around.

### 3. Ground access

 The ground unit and the van need a position within tether reach of the façade, and a closed perimeter under the flight area. A building with a car park or a lawn along its façades is simple. A tower with a busy sidewalk on all sides needs night work and traffic management, which adds cost.

### 4. Level of dirt

 A façade cleaned every year needs one pass of purified water. A façade left for five years in Bangkok traffic, or a shaded wall covered in algae, needs a treatment pass and a rinse pass. We check this during the survey, not on the day.

### 5. Material

 Glass is the fastest: heated purified water, low pressure, no detergent. Aluminium cladding and painted steel are close. Stone and concrete may need a specific product and a slower pass. Roofs and solar modules follow their own protocol. Each material has its own rate.

### 6. Permits and insurance

 In Thailand, a professional drone operation needs NBTC and CAAT registration, third-party insurance of at least 1,000,000 THB and, in urban areas or near people, a specific flight permission. CleanAlta carries these costs in its structure; a one-off job in a sensitive location (near an airport, a government building or a hospital) may require an additional permit, and that is priced separately.

## Drone versus the alternatives

 Method Cost structure Where it wins on price 

 Tethered drone Crew of 2–3 on the ground, 500–800 m²/h, no scaffolding, no anchors Large glass, cladding, roofs and solar arrays; sites that cannot close 

 Rope access Certified technicians paid per day, slow on large surfaces, roof anchors needed Small, complex or very detailed façades 

 Gondola (BMU) Low marginal cost if the building has one; blind spots on podiums and canopies Towers that already own a working BMU 

 Scaffolding Rental per week plus assembly; blocks access for weeks When repair work is done at the same time 

 Water-fed pole One operator, no permit, up to about 17 m Everything below five floors 

 A figure from France gives an order of magnitude: at Paris Saint-Lazare station, RATP reports that the drone divided the intervention time by five compared with its usual method. Time is the main cost in cleaning, so the price followed. See the RATP case study .

## How to get a reliable estimate

 Send us, through the contact page : a few photos of each façade, the address, the approximate height and number of floors, the materials, and the last time the building was cleaned. We answer with a first opinion on the right method, then a site survey before any price. Pilot sites in Thailand get a tailored offer in exchange for letting us document the job.

## Questions about cost

 Is drone cleaning cheaper than a gondola?
 If the building already has a working gondola that reaches every façade, the gondola is hard to beat on marginal cost. The drone wins where the gondola is missing, slow, or blind to podiums, canopies and glass roofs.

 Is there a minimum job size?
 In practice, a drone job is worth it from a few hundred square metres of surface. Below that, a water-fed pole is usually cheaper.

 Do you charge for the site survey?
 For buildings in Bangkok and the main regions, the survey is part of the quotation process. We say so in advance if travel costs apply.

 Does the price include water and products?
 Yes. The van produces purified water on site, and any treatment product is included in the quote.

Guide · Bangkok 

# High-rise window cleaning in Bangkok: gondola, rope access or drone?

 Bangkok adds glass towers every year along Sukhumvit, Sathorn, Silom, Ratchada and Rama 9. Most are cleaned by gondola or rope access. This guide explains what each method does well, where it fails, and where a tethered drone changes the equation.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Short answer: if your tower has a working building maintenance unit (gondola) that reaches every façade, keep using it for the main walls. Use a drone for what the gondola cannot reach: podiums, canopies, glass roofs, atriums and setbacks. If the tower has no gondola, or the gondola is out of service, a tethered drone cleans the glass at 500 to 800 m² per hour with nobody hanging in front of the units, which matters to residents and hotel guests.

## How Bangkok towers are cleaned today

 Three methods dominate. The building maintenance unit, a cradle on a roof rail, is standard on office towers and recent condominiums. Rope access, with technicians abseiling down the façade, is common on older buildings and on anything the BMU cannot reach. Traditional cleaning companies also use boom lifts and, for low buildings, water-fed poles.

 Each has a weak point. The BMU is slow, needs maintenance, and is blind to podiums and canopies. Rope access puts people at height for days, requires certified anchors, and residents do not like a technician outside their window. Boom lifts need ground space and stop at about 40 m.

## Where the drone fits

 Towers without a working BMU. Many condominiums built before 2010, and some newer ones, have no gondola or one that nobody maintains. The drone replaces rope access on the main façades.

 Podiums, canopies and glass roofs. The retail podium, the porte-cochère canopy and the lobby skylight are usually dirtier than the tower because no method reaches them easily. A drone does.

 Hotels. Nobody outside the guest rooms, work done before breakfast, no cradle noise.

 Hospitals and campuses. See how we did it at a working Paris hospital .

## Where the drone does not fit

 A tower with balconies on every floor and furniture on them; a façade on a narrow soi with no ground space for the van and perimeter; a site inside a no-fly zone near an airport without a specific permit. In those cases we propose rope access or a pole, or we decline.

## Rules in Bangkok

 A professional drone operation in Thailand needs NBTC registration of the aircraft, CAAT registration of the operator, third-party insurance of at least 1,000,000 THB, and a permission for flights in urban areas or near people. Parts of Bangkok are inside airport control zones, where flights need additional approval. CleanAlta handles this before any pilot job; details on the compliance page .

## What to do with this

 If you manage a tower in Bangkok, send us the address, the height, whether it has a BMU, and photos of the podium and canopies. We will tell you honestly which surfaces a drone would clean better, and which should stay with your current contractor.

## Questions from Bangkok building managers

 Can a drone fly between towers in Sathorn or Sukhumvit?
 Yes, as long as there is a safe ground perimeter under the flight path and the site is not in a restricted zone without permit. The tether keeps the drone within a few metres of the façade.

 Will residents see a drone outside their window?
 Briefly, a few metres away, during the pass on their floor. Unlike rope access, there is no person outside the window and no equipment left on the façade.

 Do you work at night in Bangkok?
 Night work is possible on sites that need it, as we did at Paris Saint-Lazare. It requires lighting on the façade and a specific permission.

Guide · Solar 

# Solar panel cleaning by drone in Thailand: why, how, and how often

 Rooftop solar is growing fast on Thai factories, warehouses, hotels and car parks. Dirty modules produce less, and most roofs are not safe to walk on. This guide explains what soiling costs, how a drone cleans an array without contact, and how to plan it.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Short answer: soiling from dust, pollen, soot and bird droppings reduces the output of photovoltaic modules, and the loss grows during the dry season when there is no rain to wash them. A tethered drone cleans the array from above with purified water at low pressure, with no brush, no detergent and nobody on the roof. Cleaning before the hot dry months, and again after the burning season in the north, is a reasonable starting calendar; the right frequency is set from the inverter data.

## Why dirty modules matter

 A photovoltaic module produces in proportion to the light that reaches its cells. A film of dust cuts that light; a bird dropping shades a cell and can create a hot spot that damages it. In Thailand, three things make it worse: the dry season leaves months without rain, agricultural burning in the north and north-east deposits soot, and traffic dust settles on arrays near roads and industrial estates. Low-pitch roofs and carports do not self-clean in the rain either; water pools at the lower edge and leaves a dirt line.

## Why not just send someone with a hose

 Walking on modules cracks cells and voids warranties. Tap water leaves mineral marks that reduce output themselves. Brushes scratch anti-reflective coatings. Detergents can damage seals and are prohibited by many manufacturers. And a factory roof is a fall hazard: most Thai roofs have no walkways or anchors.

## How the drone does it

 The tethered drone flies over the array, two to three metres above the modules, and sprays purified water at low pressure in passes aligned with the rows. Purified water dissolves the dirt and dries without minerals, so there is nothing to wipe. The pilot and ground crew stay on the ground. A warehouse roof of several thousand square metres is done in a day; nobody sets foot on the roof.

## How often

 It depends on the site. A reasonable starting point for a Thai industrial roof is a cleaning before the hot dry season, when soiling builds up, and a second one after the burning season for sites in the north. Arrays near a cement plant, a quarry or a busy road need more. The best indicator is the inverter data: when output on a clear day drops noticeably below the previous month at the same irradiance, it is time. See also how often to clean in a tropical climate .

## What we have done

 In France, CleanAlta cleans solar canopies and rooftop arrays with the same drone, as well as metal warehouse roofs. Photos and video on the roof and solar page .

## Questions about solar cleaning

 Does the drone touch the panels?
 No. Only water touches the modules, at low pressure. No brush, no pad, no feet.

 Can it damage the modules or the warranty?
 Purified water at low pressure is the method most manufacturers recommend. We clean early in the morning when the modules are cool, to avoid thermal shock.

 Does the plant have to be switched off?
 Usually no. We agree the procedure with the plant operator beforehand.

 Can you measure the gain?
 Yes, with the inverter data before and after, at comparable irradiance. We ask for access to it on pilot sites.

Guide · Frequency 

# How often should a façade be cleaned in a tropical climate?

 A façade in Bangkok, Phuket or Chonburi does not age like one in Paris. Heat, humidity, the monsoon, traffic soot and sea salt each leave their mark, and they do it faster. This guide gives a realistic calendar by surface, and the signs that tell you it is time.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Short answer: in Thailand, glass on a city tower generally needs cleaning two to four times a year, shaded or north-facing cladding once or twice a year before algae sets in, stone and concrete every one to three years with a treatment, tiled and metal roofs every one to two years against moss and algae, and solar modules once or twice a year depending on dust and the inverter data. Coastal buildings in Phuket, Samui, Pattaya and Hua Hin need the shorter end of each range because of salt.

## What the climate does to a building

 Humidity and shade grow algae and black mould on any surface that stays damp: north faces, walls behind trees, under canopies. The monsoon washes dust off but leaves run-off streaks under every ledge and joint. The dry season lets dust and traffic soot build up for months without rain. Sea salt on the coast dries as a film on glass and corrodes metal fixings. Heat bakes dirt onto glass and makes mineral marks from tap-water cleaning harder to remove.

## A calendar by surface

 Surface City (Bangkok, Chiang Mai, EEC) Coast (Phuket, Samui, Pattaya, Hua Hin) Signs it is overdue 

 Glass curtain wall, windows 2–4 times a year 3–4 times a year Haze in low sun, run-off streaks, salt film 

 Aluminium and composite cladding 1–2 times a year 2 times a year Grey streaks under joints, green tint on shaded faces 

 Stone, render, concrete Every 1–3 years, with treatment Every 1–2 years Black mould, green algae, dark run-off below sills 

 Tiled and metal roofs Every 1–2 years Every year Moss cushions, blocked gutters, dark patches 

 Solar modules 1–2 times a year 2 times a year Output drop at equal irradiance, dirt line at the lower edge 

 Glass roofs, atriums, canopies 2–3 times a year 3 times a year Visible from inside: dust, leaves, bird marks 

 These ranges come from our experience in France and the Thai climate data; the first pilot jobs in Thailand will refine them. They are a starting point for a maintenance plan, not a rule.

## Why frequency changes the method

 A façade cleaned regularly needs one pass of purified water, which is fast and cheap. A façade left for years needs a treatment pass, a dwell time and a rinse, which doubles the time. Regular cleaning with a fast method costs less per year than a rescue job every five years, and the building looks better in between. That is the economic case for the drone: it makes frequent cleaning affordable on surfaces where it used to be an event.

## When to plan it

 For most of Thailand, the end of the rainy season is a good time for the main clean: the dust of the dry months has not started, and the algae of the wet months is at its peak. A second clean before the hot season keeps glass clear through the months without rain. Hotels plan around occupancy; factories around shutdowns; hospitals around nothing, which is why they need a method that does not close anything.

## Questions about frequency

 Does the rain not clean the façade?
 It removes loose dust and leaves streaks of everything else. Rain does not remove algae, soot bonded by heat, or salt.

 Can CleanAlta set up a recurring contract?
 Yes. In France, Saint-Gobain Recherche moved to two passes a year after the first job. Recurring contracts get the best rate because set-up is planned.

 What about the burning season in the north?
 Soot from agricultural burning settles on everything in Chiang Mai and the north between February and April. Glass and solar modules benefit from a clean right after it.

URL: https://dronecleaningthailand.com/en/guides/tethered-drone-cleaning-how-it-works/
Guide · Method 

# How tethered drone cleaning works, step by step

 A cleaning drone is not a flying pressure washer. It is a tethered aircraft fed with power and purified water from the ground, flown by a pilot who never leaves the pavement. Here is what happens on a job, from the van to the dry glass.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Short answer: a ground unit in the van produces heated purified water and supplies power through a tether to a drone under 25 kg. The drone hovers a few metres from the façade and sprays at low pressure, then rinses. The pilot and ground crew stay inside a closed perimeter on the ground. The glass dries without streaks because purified water leaves no minerals. Cleaning rate: 500 to 800 m² per hour depending on dirt and protocol.

 Site survey. We check the façade materials, the height, where the van and ground unit can stand, the tether path, the perimeter, and the permits the site needs. Nothing is flown before this.

 Water production. The van carries a reverse-osmosis unit and a heater. Tap water goes in; purified, heated water comes out. No detergent is used on glass.

 Perimeter and briefing. Cones, tape and a ground operator close the area under the flight path. The building manager is told which entrances are affected and when.

 Tethered flight. The drone takes off from a pad, linked to the ground unit by a tether that carries power and water. It cannot fly beyond the tether, and it can stay up as long as the job needs.

 Spray and rinse. The pilot works the façade panel by panel, a few metres away, spraying at low pressure so that no glass or seal is stressed. A rinse pass leaves the surface to dry streak-free.

 Check and report. The ground operator checks the result from the ground and with the drone camera. The client receives photos before and after.

## What the drone can and cannot do

 It is excellent on large, tall, flat or gently curved surfaces: curtain walls, cladding, glass roofs, metal roofs, solar arrays. It is a poor choice for small or very detailed façades, deep balconies, and anywhere without a safe ground area below. For those, we use a 17 m water-fed pole or a 40 m aerial platform, and we say so in the quote.

## Safety in one paragraph

 The tether is the first safety device: the drone cannot fly away. The second is the perimeter: nobody stands under the flight path. The third is the crew: a pilot and at least one ground operator, both trained, with a written flight protocol and the permits for the site. In France we work under prefectoral authorisations in central Paris; in Thailand we will work under CAAT rules and NBTC registration, with the same discipline.

## See it

 The tether: power and water from the ground unit

 Purified water jet on upper-floor windows

 Inside the van: water treatment, pump and ground unit

## Questions about the method

 What is a tethered drone?
 A drone linked to a ground station by a cable that carries electrical power and, for cleaning, a water hose. It can fly for hours and cannot leave its tether radius.

 Why purified (osmosed) water?
 Tap water leaves minerals that dry as white marks. Purified water carries none, so the glass dries clean without wiping and without detergent.

 How close does the drone fly to the façade?
 Usually two to four metres, depending on the jet and the wind. The pilot adjusts the distance panel by panel.

 What happens if the wind picks up?
 Above the wind limit set in the flight protocol, the drone lands and the job waits. That is in every quote.

Glossary 

# Drone building cleaning glossary

 The words you will meet in a quote, a method statement or a Thai drone permit, explained in one or two sentences each. Alphabetical.

 By Vincent Goleau , founder of CleanAlta, professional drone pilot since 2014 Published 31 October 2026 Facts checked against sources linked in the text 

 Aerial work platform (boom lift, cherry picker)
 A truck- or trailer-mounted basket on an articulated arm. CleanAlta uses a 40 m platform for detail work and corners the drone cannot reach. Needs ground space and a flat surface.

 Algae and black mould
 Biological growth on damp, shaded surfaces: green film and black spots on cladding, render, stone and roofs. Removed with a treatment pass and a rinse, not with water alone.

 Biocide
 A product that kills moss, algae and lichen. On roofs CleanAlta applies slow-acting biocide or enzymatic treatments chosen for the material and used according to the label. Not used on glass.

 BMU (building maintenance unit, gondola, cradle)
 A suspended cradle on a roof rail or davit, used to clean and maintain tower façades. Efficient where it exists and reaches every façade; blind to podiums, canopies and setbacks.

 CAAT (Civil Aviation Authority of Thailand)
 The Thai aviation regulator. Drone operators and pilots must be registered with the CAAT; flights in cities, near people or in controlled airspace need its permission.

 Cleaning rate
 Surface cleaned per hour. CleanAlta’s tethered drone works at 500 to 800 m² per hour on glass and cladding, depending on dirt, method and protocol.

 Curtain wall
 A non-structural outer wall of glass and aluminium hung on the building frame. The typical façade of office towers and recent condominiums, and the drone’s best surface.

 Ground unit (ground station)
 The equipment on the ground that feeds the tethered drone: power supply, water pump, tether reel. Housed in or next to the van.

 Hot spot
 A cell in a solar module that overheats because it is shaded, often by a bird dropping, while the rest of the module produces. Can damage the module permanently.

 Low pressure
 Spraying at a pressure that cleans without stressing glass, seals or coatings; the opposite of pressure washing. Standard for glass, solar modules and painted surfaces.

 NBTC (National Broadcasting and Telecommunications Commission)
 The Thai regulator that registers drones as radio equipment. Every professional drone in Thailand must be registered with the NBTC as well as with the CAAT.

 Osmosed water (purified water, RO water, DI water)
 Water passed through a reverse-osmosis membrane, and sometimes a de-ionising resin, so that it contains almost no minerals. It dries on glass without marks, which is why no detergent and no wiping are needed. CleanAlta heats it for better cleaning.

 Perimeter
 The area under the flight path closed with cones, tape and a ground operator so that nobody walks under the drone. Mandatory on every CleanAlta job.

 Pilot site
 In the CleanAlta Thailand program, a building that agrees to a first, documented job in exchange for a tailored offer. See the pilot program .

 Rope access (abseiling, industrial climbing)
 Technicians working on ropes from roof anchors. Precise on complex façades, slow on large ones, and puts people at height for days.

 STS (standard scenario)
 In European drone regulation (EASA), a pre-defined operational scenario with its own training and rules. CleanAlta’s French operations follow STS-01 for urban flights. Thailand has its own framework under the CAAT.

 Tethered drone
 A drone linked to a ground unit by a cable that carries power and, for cleaning, a water hose. It can fly for hours, cannot fly away, and is the aircraft CleanAlta uses for façades and roofs. Under 25 kg in France; 24 kg on the AP-HP hospital job.

 Third-party insurance
 Insurance covering damage to people and property outside the operation. Thailand requires at least 1,000,000 THB for professional drone operations.

 Water-fed pole
 A telescopic carbon pole with a brush and purified-water feed, operated from the ground. CleanAlta’s reaches 17 m, about five floors. The cheapest method below that height.

## Boilerplate

 CleanAlta is a French building-cleaning company that uses tethered drones, water-fed poles and aerial platforms to clean façades, glass, roofs and solar panels without putting anyone at height. Founded in December 2024 by professional drone pilot Vincent Goleau, it works for clients such as RATP, AP-HP, Saint-Gobain, CNRS, CHU de Toulouse and the Paris Conservatoire. CleanAlta is preparing its launch in Thailand with a strategic partner and investors.
